questions.prompt: You have a big jug and a small test tube of the same pure, clear liquid. Which measurement could help identify the liquid, because it comes out the same for both samples?
questions.accessiblePrompt: You have a big jug and a small test tube of the same pure, clear liquid. Which measurement could help identify the liquid, because it comes out the same for both samples?

choices.text: Its mass in grams
choices.rationale: The jug holds far more liquid, so its mass is much larger; mass tells you how much you have, not what it is.

choices.text: Its volume in milliliters
choices.rationale: The jug's volume is much bigger than the test tube's; volume also depends on the amount, not the substance.

choices.text: Its boiling point at 101 kPa
choices.rationale: Correct: a pure substance boils at the same temperature at a stated pressure whether you have a lot or a little, so its boiling point is a clue to what it is.

choices.text: The time it takes to start boiling on a stove
choices.rationale: A bigger amount, or a weaker burner, takes longer to heat, so the time depends on the setup, not on the substance.

questions.conditions: Both samples are the same pure liquid, and any boiling point is measured at 101 kPa.
questions.explanation: A boiling point at a stated pressure belongs to the substance, not to the sample: a jug and a test tube of the same pure liquid boil at the same temperature. Mass, volume and heating time all change with how much liquid you have, so on their own they can't tell you what it is. That's why melting and boiling points work as clues for identifying a substance.
questions.misconception: A bigger sample has a higher boiling point, so measurements that depend on amount can identify a substance.
questions.hint: Imagine pouring half the liquid out. Which of these measurements would stay the same?
